He made a quick visit to the local hardware store that very morning, and reported that Mr. Henderson, the retired librarian, had recently bought an unusually large quantity of garden netting and wire. "No doubt about that connection," was Finn's comment, a grin spreading across his face. Then, because they had not talked to Mr. Henderson at any length, Leo questioned Finn about the appearances of the so-called Gnome King in the gardens nearby.

"He's been seen three or four times, not counting the night old Mrs. Gable swore he winked at her," Finn said. "Funny thing about the night he stole Mrs. Miller's prize fishing gnome."
"What was funny," Leo asked.
"He was alone."
"But he's always alone," Leo exclaimed.
"Nope. He's alone when he's spotted near the pond, but when he's in the gardens he has some of his little helpers with him. Sometimes one, sometimes two or three. Only saw him alone that once, the night he took the fishing gnome." This was a new angle. Leo and Finn looked at each other, puzzled.
"You've seen the others?" Finn asked.
"Sure have. Not close to, you can bet. Got no wish to tangle with garden spirits, not me. But I saw them. They walked through the azalea bushes, and they walked through Mrs. Gable's rose garden. They was lookin' for somethin'."
"How do you know?" Leo demanded.
"They'd walk, then stop, and bend over. Like they were searchin' the ground. Bet one of 'em lost a tiny hat and is huntin' for it."
"Did you see where they came from, or went to?"
"Not me. I got curiosity, but not the kind that killed that cat they tell about. Like I say, me and garden spirits don't mix, none to speak of."

Leo pondered the information. "Are these ghostly walks at twilight?"
"No. Mostly around midnight, or just after."
Leo turned to Finn. "What do you make of that?"
"Nothing," Finn replied. "Not a thing. You say you've seen as many as three men plus the Gnome King?"
"That's correct. None of them shone like the King himself, though. Most curious thing I ever saw was the night they pulled a miniature wheelbarrow, collectin' the discarded acorns from the oak tree." Leo's hair had an impulse to stand on end. The calm, factual way in which the old man piled mystery on mystery was incredible. "You mean you saw tiny figures pulling a tiny wheelbarrow?" the boy asked incredulously.
"Like I said. More a cart than a wheelbarrow, I suppose you'd say. They hauled it back and forth, and the mist trailed out behind it. Once in a while they'd stop and gather and look at the ground. Must be they were searchin' for their lost things. Don't know why else they'd need a cart. And that Crimson Hat leadin' the way every time. Up and down, back and forth."

Finn asked, "Where were you while all this was going on?"
"In my shed, scared pink, but not so scared as curious." A man of real courage, Leo thought. Believed in garden spirits, but had the nerve to watch them in action. "Mr. Henderson, you said none of them shone like the Gnome King. Did the others look solid?"
"They were dark shadows, that's all. No moon to see by, or at least not enough. Couldn't make out what they looked like."
"Has anyone else seen them in the gardens?" Finn wanted to know.
"Sure enough. Two or three that I know of, maybe more." The retired librarian paused, then asked a question of his own. "Why are you so interested in this new gnome epidemic?"
Leo considered. "It interested us," he said finally. "And it isn't making any sense."

Mr. Henderson's comment brought Leo's carefully built up assumptions tumbling down around his ears. "Oh, it makes sense, all right. He saw it once that I know of, when he was rearranging his ceramic squirrel collection." The old man added, "I was standin' right next to him at the time." Leo looked at Finn helplessly. "Thank you, Mr. Henderson," he said unhappily. "You've certainly given us plenty to think about!"

The boys watched as the old man walked back to his house, as solid and dependable as the very earth he walked on. There was no arguing with what he had seen, only with his interpretation of it. Clearly, Leo thought, he had seen figures in the gardens on several occasions. But what had the figures actually been doing? "Don't be too discouraged," Finn offered. "The old man seeing the Gnome King doesn't mean it isn't involved. Wasn't the gnome disappearance the first time the King made a public appearance? He may have been checking on the way the King looked."
"What do you suppose Henderson was doing there?" Leo asked.
"Probably just wandered over to see what was going on. I've noticed people are pretty casual about the affairs over there. No reason why Henderson wouldn't take an evening stroll to see how the neighborhood was doing."
"Well, keep our plan," Leo decided. "It's the only lead we have, so we'd better use it."

They had applied bug spray liberally, but the mosquitoes swarmed around them anyway, although bites were few. They lay quietly and watched shadow after shadow shift, but without seeing a familiar figure. During a lull in the chirping crickets, Leo asked, "Do you suppose we got here too late? He may have come earlier."
"I doubt it. Besides, where would he have parked his miniature cart? It isn't anywhere between us and the Miller's porch because we looked, and I doubt that he'd walk any farther than this." Leo had to agree that it wouldn't make much sense to park the vehicle any farther away than the spot they had selected from which to watch. The neighborhood quieted. All residents apparently had retired, and all were presumably sleeping soundly. It was only eleven o'clock; the Gnome King wasn't due for an hour. Leo thought an hour was probably more than the gnome producer needed to get ready for his appearance. Only a few minutes might be needed. That meant he and Finn would have to wait until a few minutes before midnight, to be sure no one slipped by. One late cat darted past as they waited, and then all was quiet. At ten minutes to midnight, Leo admitted defeat. "Either he isn't coming, or he got there through the bushes. Let's go see if he shows up."

As they hiked stealthily through the dark grass, ears attuned for a tiny rustle behind them, Leo explained his theory of gnome production to Finn. "There's only one way a miniature figure can be produced, and that's optically. In the movies they use a double exposure. The only way to produce an optical image on mist is with a projector of some kind."
"Gnome projector," Finn agreed. "Only where is this projector located?" That, Leo pointed out, was the prize-winning question. "All we can do is keep an eye open for the projector beam."
"Both eyes," Finn corrected. It was one minute before midnight when they arrived at Mrs. Miller's porch. The gnomes were still in their places, but there was a lack of movement or noise that made Leo aware that the gnomes knew about the King. He saw groups facing the spot where the Crimson Hat would appear. The boys were in front of the prized fishing gnome. By unspoken agreement they moved to a position directly in front of the bird bath. If the King appeared, it would be almost over their heads. The bird bath was too shallow for them to hide in, but they were in a position where any human activity couldn't possibly be overlooked.

"On your toes," Finn whispered. "Let's rush it while the Gnome King is still there." Leo swallowed hard. In spite of his conviction that a human agency, and not a supernatural one, produced the Gnome King, he didn't care much for rushing right into the apparition. In fact, he didn't like it at all. The thought of confronting a mysterious figure had felt clammy the first time, even though no harm had come to them. But, he told himself sternly, Finn was right. They either had faith in their assumptions or they didn't. "Wait until the show is almost over," Leo whispered. A voice from behind them called, "Better get out of there, you two. Rick nodded. "Good idea. And I'll take a sample of this phosphorescent material. We need proof for the authorities, solid evidence that this isn't a supernatural phenomenon. And we need to figure out where that output aperture leads."

The passage was narrow, leading through a short tunnel and then opening directly into a dense thicket of blackberry bushes and wild grapevines. Beyond the thicket, he could just make out the dark, still surface of the mill pond, glinting through the foliage. The projector was indeed perfectly positioned to cast its eerie image across the water and the low-lying mist that gathered there.

"It exits right into the prime sighting area," Rick confirmed. "Everything lines up."

After they had finished documenting everything, they carefully replaced the tarp over the cart and relocked the hidden panel in the wall, scattering fresh dirt and pebbles to hide any traces of their intrusion. They retraced their steps, moving with renewed purpose, the thrill of discovery mixed with a growing sense of danger. They had found the truth behind the ghost, but in doing so, they had stumbled into something potentially far more complex and hazardous than a simple prank.

The walk back to the car felt both shorter and longer. Shorter because their minds were alight with theories and possibilities, longer because the oppressive heat and the buzzing insects seemed to intensify with each step. They discussed their next moves in hushed tones.

"We can't just go to the police with this," Scotty reasoned. "They'll think we're crazy. 'Ghost projector in a hidden cave run by a real estate agent.' They'll laugh us out of the station."

"We need more," Rick agreed. "More proof of Collins's direct involvement, and a clearer idea of what he's actually looking for. The logbook proves the ghost is fake, but it doesn't automatically prove he's doing anything illegal besides scaring people."

"Except for trespassing and property damage, maybe," Scotty offered. "And if he's planning to claim the land, or dig something up, that could be illegal."

"Exactly," Rick said. "We need to observe him. We know his pattern now. The 'ghost' appears around nine o'clock. He needs time to set up. He's connected to the ice cream man. So, our next step is to watch Collins and the ice cream man, and see what they're actually doing when the 'ghost' is out."

They reached Rick's car, caked in mud and scratched by thorns, but buzzing with a triumphant energy. The sun was beginning its slow descent, painting the sky in hues of orange and purple.

"What about Belsely?" Scotty asked as Rick started the car. "He knows the ice cream man saw the ghost. And he says Collins knew about it. He's been observing these strange goings-on for a long time."

Someone who knew the land, its history, its value, its hidden potential. The pieces were starting to form a coherent picture, a picture far grander and more intricate than a simple local haunting. It was a picture of greed, deception, and a clever exploitation of an old legend.

"Tomorrow," Rick announced, his voice firm, "we go back to the source. We find the ice cream man, and we find Jethro Collins. And we watch them. We watch their every move."

The town lights began to appear in the distance, a comforting glow after the wild, forgotten reaches of the quarry. But Rick knew that behind the quiet facade of everyday life, a deeper mystery was still unfolding. The ghost might be fake, but the scheme behind it was very real, and potentially very dangerous. They had peered behind the curtain, and now they had to be ready for whatever revelations awaited them. The search was far from over; in fact, it had only just truly begun.

The ice cream vendor was his accomplice, perhaps even his direct operative. And the "searching" was still the key. Why go to such lengths to create a ghost that appeared to be searching? What was so valuable that it required such an elaborate and unsettling cover?
